status_reason: Material (whey and concentrate), target (protein and fat) and location (dairy process) are named, but concentrations and sample numbers are not, so the result stays provisional.
answer: For the clear whey stream, test NIR transmission/transflection; for the opaque concentrate, test NIR diffuse reflection, because transmission fails when milk is too thick or fat-rich. Keep a separate interface and calibration per stream, and compare one transflection probe on both streams as the single-interface alternative. Use independent laboratory protein and fat results as the reference.

inline.headline: Test NIR transmission/transflection on the whey and NIR reflection on the concentrate, against one transflection probe on both streams
inline.probe: transmission/transflection probe with controlled path (1-10 mm) for whey; flush-mounted diffuse reflection probe for concentrate
inline.install: whey line in a controlled-path cell; concentrate pipe or vat, flush-mounted; lab trial first
inline.fiber: silica Vis-NIR fiber (350-2400 nm), to be checked against the NIR range
inline.test_against: one NIR transflection probe used on both streams
inline.not_final_because: Transmission needs a controlled path length and fails in thick or fat-rich milk; reflection is sensitive to surface and fat globule size; the silica fiber ends at 2400 nm while NIR runs to 2500 nm; no concentrations, sample numbers or dairy accuracy figures are in the enquiry or sources.

problems.text: The whey and the concentrate need different optical interfaces (transmission/transflection for the clear whey, reflection for the opaque concentrate), so plan a separate interface decision and a separate calibration per stream; one shared interface is only a hypothesis to test.
Transmission will not work on the opaque concentrate, because light cannot penetrate thick or fat-rich milk.

Assuming the whey transmission calibration carries over to the concentrate is wrong: reflection readings depend on surface characteristics and fat globule size, so the concentrate needs its own model with MSC/SNV scatter correction before PLS.
The silica fiber range ends at 2400 nm while the NIR range runs to 2500 nm; the fiber must transmit the full method range, so confirm coverage before buying hardware.

methods.why: NIR is the most common online fiber-probe method; in dairy it is used as transmission/transflection for clear whey and reflection for opaque concentrate, with MSC/SNV and PLS for fat and protein.
It can add molecular specificity that NIR might miss, but MIR is limited to thin layers and ATR probes sample only about 1-6 µm, so test it only if NIR models fail.
It carries information complementary to NIR and suits aqueous media, but it needs special probes and strong fluorescence can mask the signal.
It depends on secondary emission that most chemicals lack, and the sources give no fat or protein fluorescence example for dairy.

questions.q: What are the protein and fat concentration ranges in the whey and in the concentrate?
questions.why: Fat-rich or thick samples decide whether transmission is possible at all and how the models must be built.

questions.q: What are the flow, temperature and pipe or vat geometry at each measuring point, and is a bypass loop possible?
questions.why: Transmission needs a controlled path length and reflection needs a flush-mounted probe.

questions.q: How many paired samples can be taken for each stream, and which lab methods give the protein and fat reference?
questions.why: Models need validated paired reference data, and the reference must be an independent lab analysis.

questions.q: Is the whey stream clear at all times, or do fat or turbidity appear during production?
questions.why: Transmission only fits transparent or semi-transparent liquids.

questions.q: Do you prefer one central analyzer with long fibers or distributed sensors at each measuring point?
questions.why: The sources state a central analyzer gives higher accuracy and distributed sensors lower installation cost, so the layout depends on your priority.

experiment.objective: Choose the interface per stream by comparing NIR transmission/transflection (whey), NIR reflection (concentrate) and one transflection probe on both streams, against independent lab protein and fat results.
steps: Collect paired samples from both streams across the production range and send each to an independent laboratory for protein and fat analysis.
Record NIR spectra of the whey with the transmission/transflection probe at a controlled path length, and of the concentrate with the flush-mounted reflection probe, using the same NIR spectrometer.
Record the same whey and concentrate samples with one transflection probe as the single-interface alternative.
Apply MSC/SNV before PLS for each stream; build separate models and validate them on samples held out from calibration.
Rank the interfaces per stream on validation error; consider a combined method only if it beats the best single method on the same validation data.
references: S01 p.17-18 (dairy NIR reflection and transmission)
S01 p.18 (both techniques on one NIR spectrometer)
S01 p.5 (building and validating chemometric models)

multispectral.why: NIR sees hydrogen bonds and polar groups, while Raman sees the molecular backbone and non-polar groups, so their information is complementary; this is a hypothesis to test after the NIR baseline.
multispectral.test: Build NIR-only and fused NIR + Raman PLS models per stream on the same validation samples for protein and fat, and keep the combination only if it predicts more accurately than the best single method.
